name: Quill
workload: Call-site latency of LOG_INFO with two ints and a double, 1 and 4 producer threads, asynchronous file logging.
claimed_speedup: Bounded dropping queue 6/9 ns vs spdlog 271/360 ns (1 thread); 8/18 ns vs spdlog 557/1106 ns (4 threads) at 50th/99.9th percentile. Also beats g3log (1066 ns) and Boost.Log (3093 ns) at 1 thread.
hardware: Intel Core i5-12600 @ 4.8 GHz, tuned system (isolcpus, nohz_full, mitigations=off), RHEL 9.4
stars_or_usage: 3.0k stars; packaged in vcpkg, Conan, Homebrew
tradeoffs: Formatting deferred to a backend thread; bounded dropping queue may drop messages; unbounded queue can grow to 64 MiB per thread (BqLog benchmark saw 2.7 GB peak at 10 threads).
caveats: Benchmark run and published by the Quill author, though code is public at odygrd/logger_benchmarks. Latency measures call site only, not end-to-end throughput; spdlog was in its default synchronous-format configuration. Backend throughput claim in a dev.to post (4.62M vs 3.46M msg/s) not opened (blocked).
found_via: WebSearch 'low latency C++ logging library benchmark faster than spdlog nanolog quill'; Quill README performance section

name: fmtlog
workload: Call-site latency for static string, concat, ints, doubles and complex format, asynchronous text logging via per-thread SPSC queues.
claimed_speedup: Own README: 6.2-6.4 ns vs spdlog basic_logger_st 156-391 ns per message. Quill README 1-thread number logging: 6/10 ns at 50th/99.9th vs spdlog 271/360 ns.
compiler_and_flags: GCC 14.2, Release, -march=x86-64-v3 (Quill benchmark); README run: GCC 10.2 tested, flags not stated
hardware: Intel Core i5-12600 @ 4.8 GHz, tuned system (isolcpus, nohz_full, mitigations=off), RHEL 9.4; README run: Xeon Gold 6144 @ 3.5 GHz
tradeoffs: Default drops messages when the 1 MB per-thread queue is full (FMTLOG_BLOCK=1 blocks instead); depends on fmt; per-callsite static info and decode function adds ~100 bytes per log statement.
caveats: Last commit Feb 2025 (about 20 months ago, so still within 'active' by a margin of a few months only). Own README compares against spdlog basic_logger_st, the synchronous logger. Tier A rests on the third-party-style Quill harness (public code, CPU, compiler, flags).
found_via: WebSearch 'fmtlog MengRao benchmark spdlog latency github'; Quill README performance table

name: XTR
workload: Call-site latency with ring-buffer producer and background formatter; formatting and I/O delegated to a consumer thread.
claimed_speedup: Quill README 1-thread number logging: 6/10 ns at 50th/99.9th vs spdlog 271/360 ns; 4 threads 8/18 ns vs spdlog 557/1106 ns. Own README: 0.894 ns for an empty log call, 1.25 ns for one int (no baseline in README).
hardware: Intel Core i5-12600 @ 4.8 GHz, tuned system (isolcpus, nohz_full, mitigations=off), RHEL 9.4
tradeoffs: Linux x86-64 only; requires a consumer thread (or user-driven polling); supports io_uring and custom sinks; depends on fmt.
caveats: Own README numbers (Ryzen 5950X, g++ 15.3.0, CPU scaling enabled warning) have no spdlog row; the spdlog comparison comes from the Quill author's harness. Sub-2 ns figures are enqueue-only in a tight loop.
found_via: Quill README performance table; WebSearch 'XTR logging library C++ low latency async github benchmark'

name: NanoLog (PlatformLab)
workload: Call-site latency with compile-time extraction of static log data, binary log output, formatting deferred offline; also throughput up to 16 threads.
claimed_speedup: Own README: 7/37 ns (50th/99.9th) for staticString vs spdlog 214/2546, glog 1198/5968, Boost 1764/3772, Log4j2 174/3364. Quill README 1-thread numbers: 8/11 ns vs spdlog 271/360.
hardware: Intel Core i5-12600 @ 4.8 GHz, tuned system (isolcpus, nohz_full, mitigations=off), RHEL 9.4
tradeoffs: Binary log needs the decompressor to read; Linux only; needs a build-time preprocessor step; custom runtime and compile pipeline.
caveats: Own README compares against spdlog v1.1.0, glog v0.3.5 and Boost 1.55, which are old; the Quill harness uses current spdlog. Last commit Dec 2020, which is stale by the 1-3 year rule if counted from Oct 2026 (nearly 6 years, so closer to abandoned).
found_via: WebSearch 'engineering blog fast C++ logger nanoseconds per log call vs spdlog glog binary logging'; NanoLog README Performance section

name: binlog
workload: Call-site latency of structured binary log event creation via lock-free queues, 1 and 4 threads (Quill harness).
claimed_speedup: Quill README 1-thread number logging: 18/119 ns at 50th/99.9th vs spdlog 271/360 ns; 4 threads 29/445 ns vs spdlog 557/1106 ns. Own README says tens of nanoseconds per event (8-38 ns in its own queue-only benchmark), with no baseline row.
hardware: Intel Core i5-12600 @ 4.8 GHz, tuned system (isolcpus, nohz_full, mitigations=off), RHEL 9.4
tradeoffs: Structured binary log needs binlog tooling to read; recovers events from coredumps; sorted-by-time reading.
caveats: Repository archived and read-only since 2026-07-01, so maintenance_status is effectively abandoned for new work. Own README benchmark measures only queue insertion with no comparison library. 99.9th percentile is worse than Quill/XTR.
found_via: WebSearch 'XTR logging library ... binlog morganstanley benchmark'; Quill README performance table

name: BqLog
workload: Total wall time for 1-10 threads each writing 2M four-parameter log entries, flushed to disk; compressed binary appender vs async spdlog, synchronous glog, fmtlog, quill, Log4j2.
claimed_speedup: BqLog Compress 95 ms vs spdlog async 560 ms at 1 thread; 507 ms vs 32939 ms at 10 threads; glog 4485 ms to 127550 ms. README summary: 6-65x faster than spdlog, 47-252x faster than glog, 7-18x faster than quill, 7-16x faster than fmtlog. Quill README call-site latency: 125/190 ns vs spdlog 271/360 ns at 1 thread (slower than Quill, XTR, fmtlog there).
compiler_and_flags: MSVC 14.51, Release x64 (per-library flags in the CMake project at the benchmark_2.5.0 tag)
tradeoffs: Fastest results are for the compressed binary appender (needs a decoder); text appender is 2.3-2.8x faster than fmtlog by its own numbers; Java/C#/Python/etc wrappers exist and are slower than the C++ API.
caveats: First-party benchmark on Windows with MSVC; the compared libraries were run with the BqLog author's configurations (glog synchronous by design, spdlog async blocking). Quill's multi-GB memory in the memory table is from its unbounded queues. Third-party Quill harness shows BqLog slower at call-site latency, so throughput win is mostly the compressed binary format. Exact MSVC flags beyond Release not stated in the doc.
found_via: Quill README performance table lists BqLog; WebFetch github.com/Tencent/BqLog

name: NanoLog (Iyengar111)
workload: Call-site latency percentiles with 1-4 threads, guaranteed (blocking) and non-guaranteed (ring buffer) modes, against spdlog, g3log, reckless.
claimed_speedup: Own README, 1 thread: nanolog_guaranteed 50th 0 us / 99.9th 8 us (avg 0.35 us) vs spdlog 3 / 11 us (avg 2.59 us) and g3log 5 / 19 us. Quill README 1-thread numbers: 106/491 ns vs spdlog 271/360 ns (faster median, worse 99.9th).
compiler_and_flags: g++ 4.8.4 (own run, flags not stated); Quill harness GCC 14.2 -march=x86-64-v3 Release
hardware: Intel i7-2630QM @ 2.0 GHz, Linux Mint 17 (own run); i5-12600 in Quill harness
tradeoffs: Header plus one cpp, C++11 only; non-guaranteed mode drops lines; text output.
caveats: License not confirmed: no LICENSE file found at the default-branch root (raw fetches returned 404), so license is null and usability reference. Different project from PlatformLab NanoLog. Own benchmark has microsecond resolution. In the Quill harness the 4-thread 99.9th percentile (1419 ns) is worse than spdlog (1106 ns).
found_via: WebSearch 'low latency C++ logging library benchmark faster than spdlog nanolog quill'; Quill README table lists 'Iyengar NanoLog'

name: haclog
workload: Front-end write time of an async C logger with a struct of u64/u32/i64/i32 and a 128-char string, stress and non-stress scenarios on 1-n threads, using Google Benchmark.
claimed_speedup: Listed among the fastest libraries in scenario 2 (fmtlog, haclog, Nanolog, quill), ahead of spdlog, glog, easyloggingpp and loguru; the comparison numbers are only in SVG charts, not text.
compiler_and_flags: GCC 14.2.1 (flags not stated; see CMakeLists.txt in the benchmark repo)
hardware: Intel i7-10710U laptop pinned to 3.2 GHz, Arch Linux, kernel 6.11.9
tradeoffs: Plain C API (callable from C++); blocks the producer when buffer full; efficiency drops sharply once the buffer fills under stress.
caveats: Benchmark repo is by the haclog author; numeric values are in chart images I did not read, so no figures are quoted; haclog is slower than fmtlog, quill and Nanolog in the stress scenario. Last commit date of haclog not shown on the page fetched.
found_via: WebSearch 'XTR logging library C++ ... benchmark' surfaced MuggleWei/cc_log_benchmark; its README

name: fastrace
workload: Cost of creating spans: 1/10/100/1000 spans and across Broadwell, Skylake, Zen and Graviton2 machines.
claimed_speedup: tokio-tracing 124x slower (Broadwell), 33x (Skylake), 36x (Zen), 29x (Graviton2) than fastrace at 3.2-4.2 us; by span count 19x/61x/124x/151x slower; rustracing 9-45x slower. OpenTelemetry SDK is not a benchmarked baseline (fastrace-opentelemetry only exports to it).
hardware: Intel Broadwell, Skylake, AMD Zen, AWS Graviton2 (machine models not given in detail)
stars_or_usage: 1.1k stars; used by Databend and Apache OpenDAL
tradeoffs: Rust-only, so not callable from C++ without FFI; no span levels; reports whole trace when the root span drops.
caveats: Baseline is Rust tokio-tracing, not spdlog/glog/OpenTelemetry SDK, so it is off-baseline for this category; compiler and flags not stated in the README; last commit date not shown in the fetched page; found via blog/crate listing.
found_via: WebSearch 'Rust tracing logging crate faster than tracing-subscriber benchmark fastrace'; fast.github.io blog (blocked); repo README
